Research problem: In MVFA's zero-shot setting there is no target data at all, so any decision threshold must be chosen on the source modalities; can split-conformal calibration of the image-level anomaly score on held-out source modalities — after replacing max-pixel aggregation with a robust, outlier-resistant pooling — provide a target false-positive rate that stays within a user-chosen bound (for example 5%) on an unseen BMAD modality, and if not, how large is the violation and which modality shifts cause it? The outcomes are the realised false-positive rate and sensitivity on each held-out modality at the conformal threshold, the coverage violation relative to the nominal level, and expected calibration error, for max pooling versus top-k-mean and quantile pooling.
Rationale: Limitations G8, G9 and G11 mean that MVFA reports only threshold-free AUC, while a deployed zero-shot detector must flag images at a fixed threshold without ever seeing labelled target data. Conformal prediction gives distribution-free guarantees only under exchangeability, which is exactly what fails across modalities; whether the guarantee approximately survives a modality shift for CLIP-based anomaly scores, and whether robust pooling of the pixel map reduces the instability caused by single spurious pixels, is an open empirical question that none of the related works address — they optimise AUROC through better features or prompts (AnomalyCLIP, HieClip, MLCA, AULoRA), and AnomalyGPT avoids thresholds only by using a fine-tuned large vision-language model. This problem differs from support-set score normalisation because it targets the zero-shot regime, where no support images exist, and asks for a guarantee rather than an improvement. It is fine-grained (only the image-level aggregation and thresholding change), inference-only, and testable on BMAD on one GPU; the leave-one-modality-out protocol is what makes the exchangeability violation measurable.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G8. Architecture, fusion, and hyperparameters are under-ablated and partly unclear: Numerous design choices — including γ = 0.1, λ = 1.0, four feature levels, an input resolution of 240, a learning rate of 10−3, a batch size of 16, 50 training epochs, β = 0.5, and fixed prompt templates — are presented without accompanying sensitivity analysis. The adapter and projector equations and their class-token handling are dimensionally unclear, and the partitioning of the 24-layer Vision Transformer into four stages is non-standard, which hinders reproducibility. The final score fusion combines zero-shot softmax probabilities on the interval [0, 1] with few-shot cosine distances on the interval [0, 2] using a fixed weight of 0.5, without normalization or calibration, so that one branch may arbitrarily dominate the fused score.
- G9. Classification and aggregation are outlier-sensitive: Image-level anomaly classification is obtained via max-aggregation over pixel-level anomaly scores, so that a single spurious high-scoring pixel is sufficient to produce a false positive. No robust aggregation, calibration, or uncertainty-estimation mechanism is employed to mitigate this sensitivity.
- G11. Metrics are too narrow for clinical readiness: Only image-level and pixel-level AUC are reported. The paper does not report Dice, IoU, or PRO scores; thresholded accuracy, F1, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, or NPV; false positives per patient; calibration or expected calibration error (ECE); or prevalence-adjusted and rare-category performance. AUC alone can obscure poor performance under severe class imbalance and does not by itself demonstrate clinical utility.

Problem: Do conformal false-positive guarantees survive a modality shift for zero-shot CLIP-based medical anomaly detection, and can they be repaired without target labels? Using MVFA trained in the leave-one-modality-out setting, we calibrate a split-conformal threshold on normal images from the source modalities (pooled, and per modality with the strictest threshold taken) at nominal false-positive levels of 1%, 5% and 10%, and measure the realised false-positive rate and sensitivity on the held-out modality, for max-pixel versus top-k-mean versus 99th-percentile image aggregation. We then test a corrective variant, weighted split conformal prediction, in which each source calibration image is weighted by a density ratio between source calibration features and the unlabelled target test batch (estimated with a domain classifier on CLIP global features), and ask whether it reduces the coverage violation. Outcomes per held-out modality: realised FPR versus nominal level, coverage violation, sensitivity at the conformal threshold, and expected calibration error.

Rationale: The reviewers asked for precise calibration sets and nominal levels, positioning against distribution-shift conformal methods, and a corrective element. The calibration sets and levels are now explicit; weighted conformal prediction, the standard correction for covariate shift, is tested in the medical VLM setting using only the unlabelled test images that a zero-shot deployment necessarily sees. The problem stays fine-grained (only aggregation and thresholding change), inference-only and runnable on one GPU, and per-modality reporting makes the answer actionable: which shifts break the guarantee and whether the weighting repairs it.
